summary: Describes network slicing for networks built from IETF technologies. It defines the term "IETF Network Slice", sets out general principles, and covers the framework for requesting and operating slices, their characteristics, and the system components and interfaces involved.

eli5.summary: Imagine one big road shared by many companies, but each gets its own reserved lane with promised speed. A network slice is that reserved lane inside a shared network.

questions: what is an ietf network slice
what is a network slice controller
subtitle: A common vocabulary and framework for network slices: connectivity between endpoints with committed performance, built on IETF technologies.

tldr.problem: Customers want connectivity like a VPN but with an assurance of specific performance, and the term "network slice" means different things in different standards bodies.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the IETF Network Slice and IETF Network Slice Service, describes them with endpoints (SDPs), connectivity constructs and service objectives (SLOs and SLEs), and sets out a framework in which a Network Slice Controller turns abstract requests into technology-specific configuration.
tldr.outcome: It gives other IETF documents consistent terms and a high-level architecture, without defining new protocols or interfaces.

facts.label: Measurable SLOs named
facts.value: 5 (bandwidth, latency, delay variation, packet loss, availability)

today: RFC 9543 is an Informational RFC with no listed obsoleting or updating documents. It supplies terminology and a framework, and leaves service interface details and specific realization technologies to other work.

sections.title: What an IETF Network Slice Is
sections.content:
Some use cases need a service that goes beyond the connectivity of a VPN by adding an assurance of meeting specific network performance objectives. The RFC calls this connectivity plus resource commitment a network slice. Because the term has wider meanings in other standards bodies, it adds the qualifier "IETF" to limit scope to networks built from IETF technologies.

An IETF Network Slice provides connectivity, with commitments of network resources, between a number of endpoints over a shared underlay network. The IETF Network Slice Service is what the customer requests and receives, and it is agnostic to the underlay technology. The slice is the provider-side realization of that service, achieved by partitioning network resources. The RFC says these two terms should be used only in this document; other documents can say "RFC 9543 Network Slice".

Services that might benefit include 5G services, network wholesale, network infrastructure sharing among operators, and NFV connectivity and data center interconnect. Evaluating existing technologies, proposing extensions and creating new protocols or interfaces are out of scope.
sections.eli5: A slice is a reserved lane with a promise about speed. The customer just asks for the lane, and the road company decides how to build it.

sections.title: Endpoints and Connectivity Constructs
sections.content:
A slice service is specified as a set of Service Demarcation Points (SDPs), one or more connectivity constructs between subsets of them, and a set of objectives for each sending SDP. An SDP is where the service is delivered to the customer, and may be a customer edge (CE) or a provider edge (PE) device, depending on the service delivery model. A CE connects to a PE over an attachment circuit (AC).

Each connectivity construct has a communication type: Point-to-Point (P2P), Point-to-Multipoint (P2MP) or Any-to-Any (A2A). A P2P construct is like a private wire or tunnel; P2MP has one sender and several receivers; A2A lets any sender reach any receiver or set of receivers, so the provider's network must work out where to deliver each packet.

More complex shapes are built from these. A bidirectional service uses two P2P constructs, and multipoint-to-point can be built from several P2P constructs. Ancillary CEs let a service include extra senders or receivers that are not customer sites, such as an IPTV or DNS server inside the provider's network, or a placeholder that is resolved when the service is instantiated.
sections.eli5: The slice connects doors where traffic goes in and out. You can have a private tube between two doors, a loudspeaker from one door to many, or a party line where any door can talk to any other.

sections.title: Objectives: SLOs and SLEs
sections.content:
A slice service is described by quantifiable Service Level Objectives (SLOs), built on Service Level Indicators (SLIs), and by unquantifiable Service Level Expectations (SLEs). Together they form the Service Level Agreement (SLA) between customer and provider. SLOs apply to a specific sending SDP and the set of receiving SDPs of a connectivity construct.

The directly measurable SLOs named are guaranteed minimum bandwidth, guaranteed maximum latency, maximum permissible delay variation, maximum permissible packet loss ratio, and availability. SLEs cannot usually be verified by the customer. Examples are security (for instance requesting encryption), geographic restrictions, maximal occupancy level, isolation and diversity. The RFC notes that if a way to verify an SLE is developed, it effectively becomes an SLO.

Slices can also be composed. In hierarchical composition a slice is further sliced, and in sequential composition slices are placed in a sequence to give an end-to-end service.
sections.eli5: Some promises can be measured, like "at least this much speed". Others are trust-me promises, like "your lane stays separate from everyone else's". Both go into the contract.

sections.title: The Framework and the Controller
sections.content:
The stakeholders are the customer, the provider, an orchestrator, the IETF Network Slice Controller (NSC) and a network controller. The customer talks to the NSC over the IETF Network Slice Service Interface, saying what is required rather than how to achieve it, and normally sees little or nothing of the provider's topology. The RFC lists security, layered implementation and scalability as benefits of this abstraction.

The NSC maps abstract requests to concrete technologies. It exposes the service interface, determines an abstract topology connecting the SDPs, maps requests to technology-specific configuration, collects telemetry, and evaluates performance against SLOs. It talks to network controllers over the Network Configuration Interface, which is technology specific. The details of the service interface are out of scope, but the RFC expects a well-defined data model including at least SDP and connectivity information, SLO/SLE specification and status.
sections.eli5: The customer tells a manager what lane they want. The manager figures out the road work and keeps checking that the lane is as fast as promised.

sections.title: Realizing a Slice
sections.content:
The architecture is deliberately high level and not prescriptive. The underlay network may be optionally narrowed into Filtered Topologies, chosen for properties such as security or geography. On top of the underlay, the operator builds Network Resource Partitions (NRPs): subsets of the buffer, queuing and scheduling resources and policies on a connected set of links. Connectivity constructs are mapped many-to-one onto NRPs.

Creating a slice follows these steps: the NSC exposes its capabilities; the customer may ask whether a service could be supported; the customer requests the service; and the NSC maps the request to network capabilities and provider policies before creating or supplementing the NRP. The definition of the service does not change whatever technology realizes it.

The RFC discusses candidate approaches without prescribing any: ACTN virtual networks, enhanced VPNs, packet marking and aggregation in IP/MPLS networks, and Service Function Chaining. It says it is inappropriate to cite unadopted proposed solutions.
sections.eli5: The road company sets aside part of each road's capacity for your lane. How it does that is up to the company, but your lane works the same either way.

sections.title: Isolation, Security and Privacy
sections.content:
Isolation means a slice is not hurt by changes in other slices or services. It may be achieved by resource partitioning from dedicated allocation to shared resources with safeguards, by VPN technologies for traffic separation, and by capacity planning, policing or shaping. Customers generally cannot tell whether an isolation SLE is met unless an SLO is breached.

The RFC states it specifies terminology and has no direct effect on the security of implementations. It raises several points: security requests in SLEs must be honoured by the underlay; an NSC needs strong authentication with each network and both interfaces need authentication, authorization and auditing; and attacking a slice by increasing traffic on another service is possible without careful planning or policing. A customer who needs confidentiality must provision their own protection, such as IPsec, or send already-encrypted traffic.

On privacy, one customer must not be able to discover the presence of other customers, and sites of one slice must not be visible outside it.
sections.eli5: Your lane should not slow down because the neighbour's lane is jammed, and nobody should be able to peek into your lane. If you need secrets kept, lock them yourself.

items.title: Guaranteed Minimum Bandwidth
items.text: SLO: minimum guaranteed bandwidth between two endpoints, measured unidirectionally in bits per second.

items.title: Guaranteed Maximum Latency
items.text: SLO: upper bound of network latency between two endpoints.

items.title: Delay Variation and Packet Loss
items.text: SLOs: maximum permissible delay variation and packet loss ratio.

items.title: Availability
items.text: SLO: ratio of uptime to the sum of uptime and downtime.

items.title: Isolation
items.text: SLE: the slice is unaffected by other services.

items.title: Security and Geography
items.text: SLEs: encryption requests and limits on where traffic is routed.
